strengths: The task is relevant to controllable image editing: evoke a specified emotion while preserving source content. Requiring only an image and target emotion provides a useful interface.

EmoPair is a potentially valuable resource, combining 331,595 existing InstructPix2Pix pairs with predicted emotion labels and 6,949 newly generated pairs. The underlying datasets and pretrained methods are credited.

The randomized human comparison provides evidence beyond classifier scores. The reported 56% aggregate online preference and several qualitative examples suggest that EmoEditor can produce useful emotional edits.
The manuscript includes component and iteration ablations, documents failure cases, and acknowledges evaluator bias and potential emotional manipulation risks.
weaknesses: The central automatic evaluation is confounded. The same predictor P labels or filters training data, guides up to 30 inference iterations, and supplies EMR, ESR, and the masks underlying ENRD. Table 1 shows EMR increasing from 5.06% without P to 50.20% with it. This establishes effectiveness against the selection criterion, but does not independently establish corresponding improvement in human emotional responses. Human evaluation of the ablations and an independent evaluator are needed.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed method's contribution. InstructPix2Pix receives single-word prompts that the paper itself identifies as ineffective. LMS improves this baseline through instruction generation, but comparisons with equivalent training data and inference-selection budgets are absent. The closely related Affective Image Filter is cited but not evaluated. These omissions leave gains from architecture, additional training, and repeated selection unresolved.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed the demonstrated novelty. The local branch uses ordinary VAE image encoding, while the global branch maps an emotion label through an MLP. Because the emotion encoder receives no source image, its alignment loss regularizes eight class-level embeddings; it does not itself demonstrate image-specific instruction reasoning or human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning. Comparisons against simpler learned or CLIP-based emotion embeddings would clarify the contribution.

Human evidence supports a modest, mixed advantage. Figure S7 reports 54% online preference against LMS, 50% for positive targets, and 49% overall in the ten-person laboratory study. Only 27% of online participants passed screening. Moreover, 417 participants completing 100 trials implies 41,700 trials, not the stated 417,000; the relationship to the retained 11,400 trials also needs clarification. The arithmetic error is correctable, but exclusion sensitivity and uncertainty accounting for repeated participants and images matter for interpreting these small margins.

Dataset quality is insufficiently validated for a principal contribution. Emotion labels come from a predictor with 73% accuracy on EmoSet, without a reported human audit of the resulting paired labels or edits. Most pairs are relabeled generic editing examples. Emotion-transition statistics and EPAS-versus-EPGS ablations would help establish coverage and the benefit of targeted curation.

The evaluation does not adequately establish the joint goal of emotional change and semantic preservation. Human participants judge emotional preference without assessing fidelity to the source. Grad-CAM masks and edge differences are not validated measures of semantic preservation; the acknowledged tiger-to-rocks failure illustrates this distinction. Within-valence editing and neutral-image generalization receive only qualitative examples, limiting the broader claims.

Important technical details remain unresolved. Section 3.2 defines the noised latent from the source image without explaining how the paired target enters the training loss. ESR uses KL divergence to a one-hot target, which is generally infinite in the stated direction unless smoothing or another convention is specified. These may be documentation errors, but they prevent verification as written. Section S2.2 also omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, sampling configuration, and inference cost; the promised future release does not currently resolve these gaps.
